about: What each place's law already says on a policy question when a game starts (2026). governing/law-in-force.ts reads it as law in force at its level (US is federal, US-XX is the state); an enacted law at the same or a higher level governs after it takes effect. A place that isn't listed for a question has no answer, which is unknown and never read as no. Dates are operative dates; a law with no date has been in force since before any game starts. A row may also carry cite (the statute or constitutional section), source (a page that supports it) and preempts: true where state law rules the question out for its cities (a preemption statute, or a question only the state answers), false where the state has no law on it and its cities may act.

US-AK.cite: Alaska Stat. ch. 34.03 (Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act)
US-AK.note: Alaska's landlord-tenant act sets no rent limit and has no bar on local rent control, and AS 34.03.310(a)(4) even protects tenants who complain to agencies enforcing governmental rent controls.

US-AZ.note: Preemption dates from 1981 and covers charter cities.

US-CA.cite: Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12 (AB 1482, Tenant Protection Act of 2019)
US-CA.note: Caps increases at 5% plus local CPI or 10%, whichever is lower, on most units 15+ years old; exempts qualifying owner-noticed single-family homes and condos; sunsets 2030-01-01.

US-CO.note: HB23-1115, which would have repealed the preemption, passed the House in 2023 but did not become law.

US-CT.note: Towns may, and towns of 25,000 or more must, create fair rent commissions that can cut an excessive rent or increase case by case, but there is no annual numeric cap.

US-DC.note: District-wide rent stabilization covers most pre-1976 units: CPI-W plus 2%, capped at 10%, once per 12 months; lower cap for registered elderly or disabled tenants.

US-DE.cite: 25 Del. C. ch. 51 et seq. (Residential Landlord-Tenant Code)
US-DE.note: Delaware's landlord-tenant code sets no general rent-increase limit and neither it nor the home-rule limits in 22 Del. C. § 835 bar local rent control; the rent-justification law covers only manufactured-home lot rents.

US-FL.note: The 2023 Live Local Act removed the former housing-emergency exception effective 2023-07-01.

US-HI.cite: Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 521 (Residential Landlord-Tenant Code)
US-HI.note: The state consumer-protection handbook says there is no limit on the amount of a rent increase because there is no rent control in Hawaii, and no statute barring county rent control was found.

US-IL.note: Enacted 1997; repeal bills (e.g., SB 1260, 2025) have not passed.

US-KY.note: Only the General Assembly may enact rent control on private property.

US-LA.note: Lessor rights may not be altered except by state law (Acts 1977, No. 655); it is an implied rather than rent-specific preemption.

US-MA.cite: Mass. G.L. c. 40P (Rent Control Prohibition Act, 1994 Question 9)
US-MA.note: The Supreme Judicial Court removed a 2026 rent-control initiative from the ballot.

US-MD.cite: Montgomery County rent stabilization law (county ordinance, 2023)
US-MD.note: Maryland has no statewide cap, and Montgomery County runs an Office of Rent Stabilization that limits increases on licensed rental units at least 23 years old.

US-ME.cite: Portland, Me., rent control ordinance (November 2020 referendum)
US-ME.note: Maine has no statewide cap, and Portland voters adopted a local ordinance that limits annual rent increases.

US-MN.note: Local rent control is prohibited unless voters approve it at a general election, which St. Paul and Minneapolis have done, so cities may act only by referendum.

US-MO.note: Preemption was broadened in August 2025 to other landlord-tenant topics.

US-MS.note: Municipalities may not regulate residential rent without prior legislative approval.

US-MT.note: Express denial of local rent-control power added in 2023 (sources name SB 105 or HB 463); opponents said it was already prohibited.

US-NE.note: Signed 2025-04-07; takes effect three months after the 2025 session adjourned (operative date computed, not stated in results).

US-NH.cite: N.H. RSA 31:39; RSA 47:17 (enumerated bylaw powers; no grant over rents); RSA 540, 540-A (no rent-limit provision)
US-NH.note: Weak: no statute bars local rent limits, but New Hampshire follows Dillon's Rule and no statute gives towns or cities power over rents.

US-NJ.cite: N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (30-year new-construction exemption); municipal police power (Helmsley v. Borough of Fort Lee, 78 N.J. 200 (1978))
US-NJ.note: The state Department of Community Affairs says New Jersey has no state law controlling rents and municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances, with new construction exempt for 30 years.

US-NV.cite: Nev. Rev. Stat. ch. 118A (NRS 118A.300 notice of rent increase)
US-NV.note: Nevada's landlord-tenant chapter requires only 60 days' notice of a rent increase and contains no bar on local rent control.

US-NY.cite: Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974 (local opt-in)
US-NY.note: The state ETPA lets a municipality adopt rent stabilization after declaring a local housing emergency, so limits apply only in New York City and opt-in localities.

US-OH.note: HB 430 added an express preemption of local rent control and rent stabilization.

US-OR.note: Cap is 7% plus CPI; SB 611 (effective 2023-07-06) added a 10% ceiling; units under 15 years old are exempt; ORS 91.225 still preempts local rent control.

US-PA.note: Weak: no statute bans rent control, but the home-rule law and Dillon's Rule keep cities from capping rents.

US-RI.note: Rhode Island requires only 60 days' notice of a rent increase (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62) and has no statute barring local rent control.

US-TX.note: Cities may impose rent control only in a disaster-declared housing emergency with the governor's approval.

US-UT.note: Local rent control requires express legislative approval.

US-VA.cite: Va. Code § 55.1-1200 et seq. (VRLTA supersession) with Dillon Rule
US-VA.note: No rent-specific preemption statute; localities lack authority because the VRLTA supersedes local landlord-tenant ordinances, and 2026 bills HB 278/SB 355 to authorize local rent regulation were sent to study.

US-VT.note: Vermont's rental chapter, current through the 2025 session, has no rent cap and no bar on local rent control, though a city would need a charter change approved by the legislature.

US-WA.note: Cap is the lesser of 7% plus CPI or 10% over 12 months (9.683% for 2026); new construction under 15 years exempt; expires 2040-07-01; RCW 35.21.830 still preempts local rent control.

US-WV.note: Untested: no statute bars local rent limits and cities have broad powers (§ 8-12-5(43)), though § 8-1-5a(k) could be read against a cap.

US-WY.cite: Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 to -1211 (Residential Rental Property Act)
US-WY.note: No rent-control preemption appears in Wyoming's landlord-tenant, municipal (Title 15) or property (Title 34) statutes as compiled in May 2026, so the claim of a preemption statute is unsupported.

US-AK.note: Section 12.30.011(b) lets the judge require a cash appearance bond, a bail bond with sureties or a cash performance bond; HB 49 (2019) repealed SB 91's release presumptions.

US-AL.note: Rule 7.2 lets the court release on recognizance or an appearance bond and refers to secured appearance bonds; money bail remains a standard condition.

US-AZ.note: Section 13-3967 lets the judge require a deposit of cash or other security as a release condition.

US-CA.note: Bail is accepted in cash or surety bond under countywide bail schedules; voters rejected SB 10's replacement of cash bail (Proposition 25, November 2020).

US-CO.note: Section 16-4-104 still authorizes a bond with secured monetary conditions, although unsecured personal recognizance bonds come first.

US-CT.note: Practice Book § 38-4 lists 7 percent cash bail and bonds with surety among release conditions and bars judges from prohibiting surety bonds; the statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-64a) could not be fetched from cga.ct.gov.

US-DC.note: A judge may not set a financial condition that results in detention, so money bail is effectively unused (provision dates from the 1992 amendments). H.R. 5214 (D.C. Cash Bail Reform Act) passed the House on 11/19/2025 but had not passed the Senate, so it was not law on 1/1/2026 (GovTrack, https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/119/hr5214).

US-DE.note: Delaware prefers nonmonetary conditions but still authorizes bonds guaranteed by financial terms, including cash-only bonds.

US-FL.note: Florida law sets bail criteria and requires monetary bonds of at least $2,000 in certain failure-to-appear cases.

US-GU.note: Section 40.20(d) authorizes a bond secured by cash, other property or qualified sureties; the compilation is current to 6/24/2021.

US-HI.note: Section 804-9 has judges set a reasonable bail amount considering ability to afford it; money bail remains lawful.

US-IA.note: Section 811.2 authorizes cash deposits and bail bonds with sufficient surety as release conditions.

US-ID.note: The Idaho Bail Act defines bail as a monetary amount required for release and regulates bail agents and bail bonds.

US-IL.note: The Pretrial Fairness Act (SAFE-T Act, P.A. 101-652) abolished monetary bail on 9/18/2023; release is decided by conditions or a detention hearing. The statute page on ilga.gov could not be fetched (TLS failure / egress block), so the source is secondary.

US-IN.note: Rule 2.6 (effective 1/1/2024) favors release without money bail for low-risk arrestees but expressly authorizes money bail by surety bond or cash deposit.

US-KS.note: Section 22-2802 authorizes appearance bonds with sureties and cash bonds.

US-KY.note: Partial: Kentucky bans commercial bail bondsmen and presumes release on unsecured bond for low- and moderate-risk defendants, but courts still set bail and the statute credits jail time toward it.

US-LA.note: Article 321 lists commercial surety, secured personal surety and cash deposit among the types of bail.

US-MA.note: Section 58 presumes personal recognizance but allows cash bail (or an equivalent surety bond) set with regard to financial resources.

US-MD.note: Section 5-205 lets District Court judges set bond or bail, including cash bail; Maryland's 2017 court rule favors nonfinancial conditions but did not abolish money bail.

US-ME.note: Section 1026 lets the judicial officer require a bail bond with sureties or a financial condition, considering ability to pay.

US-MI.note: Section 765.6 has the court fix a bail amount, with 10 percent deposit or surety bonds.

US-MN.note: Rule 6.02 lets the court require an appearance bond, cash deposit or other security when recognizance is not enough.

US-MO.note: Section 544.455 lets the judge require a bail bond with sureties or a cash deposit.

US-MP.note: Rule 46 lets the judge require an appearance bond with a cash deposit or a bail bond with sureties.

US-MS.note: Rule 8 provides for secured appearance bonds and publishes recommended money bond ranges.

US-MT.note: Section 46-9-401 lists cash deposits, real estate pledges and surety bonds as forms of bail.

US-NC.note: Section 15A-534 authorizes secured appearance bonds backed by cash, mortgage or surety.

US-ND.note: Rule 46 lets the magistrate require an appearance bond with a cash deposit or other security.

US-NE.note: Section 29-901 authorizes appearance bonds with a cash deposit of up to 10 percent, or full bail bonds.

US-NH.note: Section 597:2 authorizes cash or corporate surety bail, set considering ability to post it.

US-NJ.note: Partial but near-abolition: the Criminal Justice Reform Act relies primarily on non-monetary release and allows monetary bail only when no other condition will assure appearance; it took effect with the 2014 amendment to N.J. Const. art. I, para. 11 (January 1, 2017).

US-NM.note: Partial: the 2016 amendment (SJR 1) allows felony detention without bail and bars holding someone solely for inability to post a money or property bond, but keeps bail by sufficient sureties.

US-NV.note: Section 178.502 lets the court require sureties or accept cash for a bail bond.

US-NY.note: Partial: since 1/1/2020 money bail is barred for most misdemeanors and nonviolent felonies, but it remains a standard condition for qualifying offenses (list since expanded); nysenate.gov refused the fetch, so the source is secondary.

US-OH.note: Section 2937.22 lists deposits of cash and bonds and surety undertakings as forms of bail.

US-OK.note: The constitution makes all persons bailable by sufficient sureties (with listed exceptions); the statutes (22 O.S. § 1105) could not be fetched from oscn.net or oklegislature.gov.

US-OR.note: Partial: Oregon has no commercial bail bonds, but security release requires depositing 10 percent of a money security amount set by the magistrate.

US-PA.note: Rule 524 lists monetary conditions and full cash bail among the types of release on bail.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Const. art. II, § 11; P.R. R. Crim. P. 218
US-PR.note: The constitution guarantees admission to bail before conviction and bars excessive bail; bail (fianza) is a money amount. Rule 218 itself could not be fetched.

US-RI.note: Section 12-13-1 releases defendants upon recognizance with sufficient surety or sureties.

US-SC.note: Section 17-15-10 lets the court require an appearance bond with good and sufficient sureties.

US-SD.note: Section 23A-43-3 lets the court require an appearance bond backed by a cash or security deposit.

US-TN.note: The constitution makes all prisoners bailable by sufficient sureties; Tennessee's code (Tenn. Code Ann. tit. 40, ch. 11) is not on a fetchable official site.

US-TX.cite: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. ch. 17 (as amended by S.B. 6, 87th Leg., 2d C.S., 2021)
US-TX.note: S.B. 6 (2021) regulates setting bail amounts and restricts release on personal bond for certain defendants, so monetary bail remains standard.

US-UT.note: Section 77-20-205 lists a financial condition among release conditions; the fetched page is the version effective 5/6/2026, and the financial-condition option also existed on 1/1/2026.

US-VA.note: Section 19.2-123 authorizes secure bonds satisfied by sureties or cash.

US-VT.note: Section 7554 lets the judicial officer require a secured appearance bond or surety bond, considering financial means.

US-WA.note: CrR 3.2 lets the court require a bond with a cash or security deposit or a surety bond.

US-WI.note: Partial: Wisconsin bars commercial bail bonds, but judges may require bail bonds with sureties or cash deposits.

US-WV.note: Article 1C governs admission to bail and review of the amount of bail; money bail remains lawful.

US-WY.note: Title 7, ch. 10 governs bail amounts, sureties and forfeiture of bail (details in W.R.Cr.P. 46.1).

US-AL.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may vote a regular ballot if two poll workers identify the voter.

US-AR.note: Strict photo: Act 249 of 2021 removed the affidavit fail-safe, so a voter without photo ID votes provisionally and must show ID by noon the Monday after the election.

US-AZ.note: Strict non-photo: photo ID or two non-photo documents with name and address.

US-CA.note: No document required at the polls (first-time voters under federal law excepted).

US-CO.note: Non-photo ID accepted; 2025 SB 1 added more non-photo IDs.

US-CT.note: Non-strict non-photo ID; a voter may sign an affidavit.

US-DC.note: No document required at the polls.

US-DE.note: Non-strict non-photo ID; a voter may sign an affidavit.

US-FL.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID casts a provisional ballot that counts if the signature matches the registration record.

US-GA.note: Strict photo; 2025 HB 296 requires a driver's license used for voting to be a physical card.

US-GU.note: The Guam Election Commission states voters must present a photo ID issued by a federal, state, Guam school or government of Guam entity to vote; the exact 3 GCA section was not confirmed.

US-HI.note: Act 136 of 2019 repealed the rule that voters show ID on request; no ID is required except as federal law requires.

US-IA.note: Non-strict non-photo: the non-photo Iowa voter ID card is accepted.

US-ID.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without ID may sign an affidavit and vote; 2023 HB 124 removed student IDs, and 2026 SB 1322 (effective 07/01/2026) adds verification data to the affidavit.

US-IL.note: No document required at the polls.

US-KY.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and show a secondary ID; SB 154 later narrows the accepted secondary IDs starting in 2026.

US-LA.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-MA.note: No document required at the polls.

US-MD.note: No document required at the polls.

US-ME.note: No document required at the polls; a voter ID ballot question failed in November 2025.

US-MI.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-MN.note: No document required at the polls.

US-MO.note: Non-strict photo in part: 2022 HB 1878 removed non-photo alternatives; a voter without photo ID votes provisionally, and the ballot counts if the signature matches or the voter returns with ID.

US-MP.note: The Commonwealth Election Commission pamphlet says a pictured ID is required to be issued a ballot at the polls; the statute located covers early voting.

US-MT.note: Non-strict non-photo: a utility bill or other document with name and address is accepted; the 2024 Montana Supreme Court ruling kept student IDs.

US-NC.note: Photo ID in force since the 2023 municipal elections; a voter without one may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and cast a provisional ballot that counts unless the declaration is found false.

US-ND.note: Strict non-photo: ID must show a residential address but need not bear a photo.

US-NE.note: Strict photo with a reasonable impediment certification for voters who cannot obtain ID. Signed 6/1/2023 (LB 514); first applied at the 5/14/2024 primary.

US-NH.note: Photo ID has been asked for years; HB 1569 made it strict by removing the ID affidavit effective 11/11/2024, and HB 323 drops student IDs effective 06/02/2026.

US-NJ.note: No document required at the polls.

US-NM.note: No document required at the polls; a voter may state identifying information verbally.

US-NV.note: No document required; AB 499 (photo ID) was vetoed on 06/12/2025, and a photo ID constitutional amendment faces its second vote in November 2026.

US-NY.note: No document required at the polls.

US-OH.note: Strict photo under HB 458; a voter without photo ID votes provisionally and must show ID within four days.

US-OK.note: Non-strict non-photo: the non-photo voter identification card is accepted.

US-PA.note: No document required except for first-time voters at a polling place.

US-PR.note: The 2020 Electoral Code names the photo electoral ID card or other listed photo IDs as the identification valid for voting; the fallback for a voter with none was not confirmed.

US-RI.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID casts a provisional ballot that counts if the signature matches.

US-SC.note: Non-strict photo: a voter with a reasonable impediment may sign an affidavit, show the non-photo registration card and vote provisionally.

US-SD.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-TX.note: Non-strict photo: a voter who cannot reasonably obtain photo ID may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and show a supporting document.

US-UT.note: Non-photo documents accepted in person; 2025 HB 300 changes mail-ballot ID, not the in-person photo question.

US-VA.note: Non-strict non-photo since the 2020 repeal of photo ID.

US-VT.note: No document required at the polls.

US-WA.note: A voting-center voter may either provide ID or sign a ballot declaration, so no document is required.

US-WI.cite: Wis. Stat. § 6.79(2); Wis. Const. art. III, § 1
US-WI.note: Strict photo; voters constitutionalized the requirement in April 2025.

US-WV.note: Non-strict photo: HB 3016 replaced non-photo ID with photo ID effective 07/11/2025; a poll worker who has known the voter for six months may vouch, and others vote provisionally after an affidavit.

US-WY.note: Strict non-photo per NCSL: the 2021 law (HB 75) mostly lists photo IDs but also accepts Medicare and Medicaid cards.

US-AL.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-AR.note: Twelve consecutive years total in the General Assembly for members first elected on or after 1/1/2021, eligible again after a four-year break; earlier members use a 16-year aggregate (2014 and 2020 amendments, 2020 Issue 2).

US-AS.note: Fono senators and representatives are not subject to term limits.

US-AZ.note: Eight years (four two-year terms) in each chamber, consecutive; adopted 1992.

US-CA.note: Twelve years total in either or both chambers, lifetime (2012 Proposition 28, approved 6/5/2012).

US-CO.note: Eight years in each chamber (four House terms, two Senate terms), consecutive; adopted 1990.

US-CT.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-DC.note: D.C. Councilmembers serve four-year terms with no limit.

US-DE.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-FL.note: Eight years in each chamber, consecutive; adopted 1992.

US-GA.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-GU.note: Guam senators serve two-year terms without term limits; proposed bills were not enacted.

US-HI.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-IA.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-ID.note: Voters adopted limits in 1994, but the legislature repealed them in 2002.

US-IL.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-IN.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-KS.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-MD.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-NH.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-NJ.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-VA.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-VI.note: Virgin Islands senators serve two-year terms without term limits.

US-VT.note: No term limit for state legislators.

US-WI.note: No term limit for state legislators.

us-policy-positions:government-operation.source: NCSL redistricting commission summaries (legislative and congressional), Ballotpedia redistricting procedures and commissions pages, Brennan Center 'Who Draws the Maps?', state constitutions (AK, MT, PR, CNMI), Ballotpedia on California Prop 50 (11/2025), Utah Prop 4 litigation (11/2025) and Virginia's April 2026 amendment; searched 9/28/2026.

US-AK.note: The five-member Redistricting Board, whose members may not be public employees or officials, adopts the legislative maps with final authority; Alaska has one congressional district. It lacks an independent screening panel, so the Brennan Center's stricter test is not fully met.

US-AL.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-AR.note: The Board of Apportionment (governor, secretary of state, attorney general) draws legislative maps, which is a politician commission; the legislature draws the congressional map.

US-AZ.note: The Independent Redistricting Commission draws both congressional and legislative maps with final authority (Proposition 106).

US-CA.note: The Citizens Redistricting Commission draws the legislative and Board of Equalization maps with final authority. Proposition 50 (approved 11/4/2025) substitutes a legislature-drawn congressional map for the 2026, 2028 and 2030 elections, and the commission resumes congressional redistricting in 2031.

US-CO.note: Separate independent congressional and legislative commissions draw the maps with final authority, subject to state supreme court review (Amendments Y and Z).

US-CT.note: The legislature draws maps; a backup commission of legislative-leader appointees acts only if it fails, and the Supreme Court acts after that.

US-DC.note: The D.C. Council redraws ward boundaries by legislation; there is no independent commission.

US-DE.note: The legislature draws the legislative map; Delaware has one congressional district.

US-FL.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-GA.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-GU.note: Guam's 15 senators are elected at large; there are no districts and no redistricting commission.

US-HI.note: The nine-member Reapportionment Commission is appointed by legislative leaders and has no bar on officials serving, so national sources class it as a politician commission, although it has final authority over both maps.

US-IA.note: Nonpartisan Legislative Services Agency staff prepare plans, but the legislature must approve them.

US-ID.note: The Commission for Reapportionment, whose members may not be elected officials, draws both congressional and legislative maps with final authority (1994 amendment).

US-IL.note: The legislature draws maps; a backup commission including legislators acts only if the legislature fails on the legislative map.

US-IN.note: The legislature draws maps; a backup politician commission acts only for congressional maps if the legislature fails.

US-KS.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-KY.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-LA.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-MA.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-MD.note: The legislature draws maps; the governor's redistricting advisory commission only recommends.

US-ME.note: The legislature enacts the maps (by two-thirds vote); the apportionment commission is advisory, with the supreme court as backup.

US-MI.note: The Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission draws both congressional and legislative maps with final authority (Proposal 2 of 2018).

US-MN.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps, with courts acting when it deadlocks.

US-MO.note: The legislature draws the congressional map; legislative maps are drawn by bipartisan commissions nominated by party committees and appointed by the governor (Amendment 3 of 2020), which the Brennan Center treats as a political commission, not an independent one.

US-MP.cite: N. Mar. I. Const. art. II, § 4
US-MP.note: The legislature reapportions the House of Representatives, and the governor acts if it fails; there is no independent commission.

US-MS.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-MT.note: The Districting and Apportionment Commission files final congressional and legislative plans; the legislature may only recommend changes to the legislative plan.

US-NC.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps, not subject to governor veto.

US-ND.note: The legislature draws the legislative map; North Dakota has one congressional district.

US-NE.note: The unicameral legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-NH.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-NJ.note: Congressional and legislative maps are drawn by commissions appointed by party leaders on which elected officials may serve, which national sources class as politician commissions.

US-NM.note: The legislature draws maps; the Citizen Redistricting Committee created in 2021 is advisory only.

US-NV.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-NY.note: The Independent Redistricting Commission is advisory; the legislature may reject its plans and draw its own.

US-OH.note: Legislative maps are drawn by the Ohio Redistricting Commission of statewide officials and legislators (a politician commission), and the legislature draws congressional maps first; Issue 1 to create a citizen commission failed in 2024.

US-OK.note: The legislature draws maps; a politician backup commission acts only if it fails on legislative maps.

US-OR.note: The legislature draws maps; the secretary of state acts as backup for legislative maps.

US-PA.note: The Legislative Reapportionment Commission of four legislative leaders plus a chair draws legislative maps (a politician commission); the legislature draws the congressional map.

US-PR.note: Senatorial and representative districts are revised after each census by a board of the Chief Justice and two governor-appointed members of different parties, not legislators; national classifications do not cover Puerto Rico, which has no voting congressional districts.

US-RI.note: The legislature draws maps; any commission is advisory.

US-SC.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-SD.note: The legislature draws the legislative map; South Dakota has one congressional district.

US-TN.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-TX.note: The legislature draws maps; the Legislative Redistricting Board of statewide officials acts as backup for legislative maps.

US-UT.note: The legislature draws the maps; the Independent Redistricting Commission from Proposition 4 (2018) is advisory. On 11/10/2025 a state district court rejected the legislature's congressional map under Proposition 4 and imposed a court-chosen map, but that did not give the commission final authority.

US-VA.note: The 2020 Virginia Redistricting Commission is half legislators, and the maps go to the General Assembly and then to the state supreme court if the commission fails. An 4/21/2026 referendum that would have let the legislature redraw congressional maps was voided by the state supreme court on 5/8/2026.

US-VI.note: Legislative districts are fixed by the Revised Organic Act and territorial law (St. Croix; St. Thomas/St. John; St. John at-large seat); there is no redistricting commission.

US-VT.note: The legislature draws the legislative map with an advisory apportionment board; Vermont has one congressional district.

US-WA.note: The Washington State Redistricting Commission draws both congressional and legislative maps; the legislature may amend an adopted plan only by a two-thirds vote, affecting no more than 2 percent of a district's population.

US-WI.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps, subject to governor veto.

US-WV.note: The legislature draws congressional and legislative maps.

US-WY.note: The legislature draws the legislative map; Wyoming has one congressional district.

us-policy-positions:fiscal.graduated-inc.source: Tax Foundation, 2026 State Income Tax Rates and Brackets (as of 02/11/2026), 2023/2024/2025 editions and 2026 State Tax Changes; state statutes and agency pages fetched 09/28/2026 (azdor.gov, dor.georgia.gov, legis.iowa.gov, revenue.louisiana.gov, dor.ms.gov, ncleg.gov, apps.legislature.ky.gov, le.utah.gov, legislature.idaho.gov, codes.ohio.gov, legislature.mi.gov, tax.illinois.gov, pa.gov, palegis.us, malegislature.gov, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov); territories: IRS Publication 570 (2025), hacienda.pr.gov 2025 instructions, cnmilaw.gov, americansamoa.gov Tax Office.

US-AS.note: The American Samoa Government Tax Office publishes the IRS 2000 Tax Table and Instructions for use with Form 390, with graduated rates (15 percent and up); IRS Publication 570 (2025) says its tax laws are modeled on the Internal Revenue Code with certain differences.

US-AZ.note: Flat 2.5 percent from tax year 2023 (Arizona Form 140 instructions for 2023 tell filers to multiply taxable income by 2.5 percent; Tax Foundation says S.B. 1828 triggers reached the flat rate a year early). The A.R.S. 43-1011 page served by azleg.gov did not show the flat-rate paragraph, so no cite is given.

US-CO.note: Single 4.4 percent rate for 2026; flat structure predates 2000 (not re-verified from a primary page because tax.colorado.gov refused the request, so no cite is given).

US-GA.note: Flat rate from 01/01/2024 (5.39 percent for 2024 per the Georgia IT-511 booklet; 5.19 percent in the Tax Foundation 2026 table), replacing a graduated tax with a 5.75 percent top rate.

US-GU.note: IRS Publication 570 (2025) says Guam has its own tax system based on the same tax laws and tax rates that apply in the United States (seven graduated federal brackets); the Guam Department of Revenue and Taxation administers it as the Guam Territorial Income Tax.

US-IA.note: Iowa Code 2026 section 422.5 imposes one rate of 3.8 percent; Tax Foundation reports the three brackets were consolidated into that single rate effective 01/01/2025.

US-ID.note: Section 63-3024 was added by the 2022 First Extraordinary Session (HB 1), replacing brackets with one rate above an exempt band for tax year 2023 (Tax Foundation gives the bill an effective date of 01/03/2023); the rate is now 5.3 percent.

US-IL.note: The Illinois Department of Revenue lists one individual rate of 4.95 percent effective 07/01/2017; the single-rate structure predates 2000 (ilga.gov failed TLS verification, so no statute or constitution cite is given).

US-IN.note: Single 2.95 percent state rate for 2026; flat structure predates 2000 (no primary statute page could be fetched, so no cite is given).

US-KY.note: 2018 HB 487 amended KRS 141.020 to a single 5 percent rate for taxable years beginning on or after 01/01/2018, replacing six brackets; the Tax Foundation 2026 table shows 3.5 percent.

US-LA.note: The Louisiana Department of Revenue says tax years beginning on or after 01/01/2025 use a flat 3 percent rate, replacing 1.85/3.5/4.25 percent brackets; no fetched page supported a statute cite.

US-MA.cite: Mass. Const. amend. art. 44, as amended by art. 121
US-MA.note: The base rate is a flat 5 percent, but Article CXXI adds a 4 percent surtax on income over an inflation-adjusted $1,000,000 for tax years beginning on or after 01/01/2023.

US-MI.note: MCL 206.51 sets one rate (4.25 percent since 10/01/2012, with revenue-trigger reductions); the single-rate structure predates 2000.

US-MP.note: The CNMI wage and salary tax (4 CMC 1204, from PL 9-22) applies rates from 2 to 9 percent by wage level, and 4 CMC 1701 adopts the Internal Revenue Code as the Northern Marianas Territorial Income Tax.

US-MS.note: H.B. 531 (2022) removed the 4 percent band from 01/01/2023, leaving 0 percent on the first $10,000 and one positive rate above it (4 percent for 2026 per the Mississippi Department of Revenue); no fetched page supported a statute cite.

US-MT.note: Two brackets remain for tax year 2026; the top rate fell to 5.65 percent.

US-NC.note: Session Law 2013-316 enacted G.S. 105-153.7 with one 5.8 percent rate for taxable years beginning on or after 01/01/2014; the rate is 3.99 percent after 2025.

US-ND.note: A zero-rate band sits below two positive rates, so the tax is graduated.

US-NH.note: No tax on wages; the separate tax on interest and dividends ended for tax years from 01/01/2025.

US-OH.note: HB 96 (2025) amended section 5747.02 so that for taxable years beginning in 2026 nonbusiness income over $26,050 is taxed at one 2.75 percent rate (income at or below $26,050 is exempt); 2025 still had 2.75 and 3.125 percent brackets.

US-OK.note: HB 2764 collapsed six brackets into three (2.5, 3.5 and 4.5 percent) on 01/01/2026; the tax stays graduated.

US-PA.note: The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue levies one 3.07 percent rate; the constitution requires taxes to be uniform on the same class of subjects. Single rate predates 2000.

US-PR.note: Hacienda 2025 individual return instructions give graduated normal-tax brackets of 0, 7, 14, 25 and 33 percent under section 1021.01; no 2026 change to a single rate was found.

US-UT.note: 2007 S.B. 223 ended graduated brackets for taxable years beginning on or after 01/01/2008. Tax Foundation lists 4.5 percent for 2026; the current Utah Code section 59-10-104, amended in the 2026 General Session and shown as effective 01/01/2026, sets 4.45 percent.

US-VI.note: IRS Publication 570 (2025) says the USVI has its own tax system based on the same tax laws and tax rates that apply in the United States, so wages face the graduated federal schedule; residents file Form 1040 with the Virgin Islands Bureau of Internal Revenue.

US-WA.note: No tax on wages; the capital gains excise tax adopted in 2021 does not count as a wage income tax.

US-AK.note: Ketchikan Public Utilities, a city utility, sells retail internet and phone service; no Alaska statute barring it was found.

US-AL.note: Act 2000-614 lets municipal providers offer internet only within set territorial limits, requires hearings, and limits financing to revenue-backed debt; text read from the ALISON official code service.

US-AR.cite: Ark. Code Ann. § 23-17-409(b) (as amended by Act 67 of 2021)
US-AR.note: Act 67 of 2021 (SB 74, not Act 764 as in the draft) lets any government entity own and operate broadband facilities; bond- or tax-funded projects still need a private operating partner, a hearing and any election the bond law requires.

US-CA.note: Municipal corporations may operate public utilities supplying their inhabitants with means of communication.

US-CO.note: SB23-183 repealed the 2005 requirement that a local government win a referendum before offering broadband.

US-FL.note: A governmental entity must hold two public hearings, adopt a business plan and meet break-even and enterprise-fund conditions before it sells communications service; 2025 statutes text.

US-GA.note: The City of Thomasville lists CNSNext digital TV, telephone and high-speed internet among its city utility services.

US-IA.note: Establishing a city utility, including a telecommunications system, needs voter approval (§ 388.2), and § 388.10 bars general-fund or cross-utility subsidy of city telecommunications; trackers do not list Iowa (see conflicts).

US-ID.note: Idaho Falls Fiber, owned by the city's Idaho Falls Power, runs a fiber network serving homes and businesses on an open-access model with private retail providers.

US-IL.note: Rochelle Municipal Utilities, a city utility, sells fiber internet and phone service to homes and businesses.

US-IN.note: Auburn Essential Services, a City of Auburn department, sells residential internet plans up to multi-gigabit fiber.

US-KS.note: The City of Coffeyville sells Coffeyville Fiber Internet service; the cited notice (4/7/2026) announces updated rates for an existing service.

US-KY.note: The Frankfort Plant Board, a municipal utility, sells fiber internet, cable TV and telephone service.

US-LA.note: The Local Government Fair Competition Act bars a local government from providing cable, telecommunications or advanced service except as the chapter allows (feasibility, election and cost conditions).

US-MA.note: A municipal lighting plant may build and operate a telecommunications system for its customers; debt needs a town vote under ch. 44 as for any plant debt.

US-MD.note: Easton Utilities, the Town of Easton's utility commission, sells internet, TV and phone service alongside electric, gas and water.

US-MI.note: A public entity may provide telecommunication service only after it seeks bids and receives fewer than three qualified private bids; unamended since 2005 per the MCL page current through PA 103 of 2026.

US-MN.cite: Minn. Stat. § 237.19 (as amended by 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 114, art. 4, § 2)
US-MN.note: The 2024 amendment removed the 65 percent supermajority election that had been required before a municipality could provide telecommunications service.

US-MO.note: Political subdivisions may not sell certificated telecommunications service or facilities to the public, though the subsection exempts internet-type services, so the bar mainly reaches voice and bundled service.

US-MT.note: A political subdivision may be an internet service provider only where no private provider is available (or for services it offered before 7/1/2001); the 2025 code keeps this after 2021, 2023 and 2025 amendments.

US-NC.note: Session Law 2011-84 imposes cost-imputation, enterprise-fund, special-election (before debt) and service-area conditions on city-owned communications service; a 2025 amendment (S.L. 2025-25) only touched definitions.

US-NE.note: An agency or political subdivision that is not a public power supplier may not provide broadband, internet, telecommunications or video service at retail or wholesale (LB 645, 2005; amended 2021).

US-NH.note: Municipalities may bond for broadband infrastructure only in locations unserved by broadband and only after a request for information to incumbent providers; national trackers do not list New Hampshire (see conflicts).

US-NV.note: Cities of 25,000 or more and counties of 55,000 or more may not sell telecommunication service to the general public.

US-OH.note: FairlawnGig, the City of Fairlawn's municipal broadband utility, sells residential and business fiber internet.

US-OK.note: The City of Sallisaw's DiamondNet sells fiber internet and phone service over city-owned fiber.

US-OR.note: SandyNet, a City of Sandy public utility, is the local internet service provider, selling fiber and wireless service.

US-PA.note: A political subdivision may not sell broadband in an incumbent's territory unless the incumbent declines a written request for the speeds sought; current consolidated text.

US-SC.note: Government-owned communications providers must meet tax-equivalent payments, cost-imputation and no-subsidy rules (2002 Act 360, 2012 Act 284), with relief only for designated unserved areas.

US-TN.note: Municipal electric systems may offer broadband only within their electric service area; the Sixth Circuit (2016) reinstated this limit after the FCC's preemption. The current code text was not reachable (official host requires JavaScript), so the 2026 status rests on this 2016 ruling.

US-TX.note: A municipality or municipal electric system may not sell certificated telecommunications service to the public (1997; amended 2005); the official Texas statutes site serves a JavaScript shell, so a mirror citing it was used.

US-UT.note: The Municipal Cable Television and Communications Services Act requires feasibility studies, hearings and a revenue-over-cost test before a municipality offers broadband; 2025 amendments (effective 5/7/2025) kept and extended it.

US-VA.note: Localities with electric systems need a commission certificate and must impute taxes and fees and avoid cross-subsidy when selling telecommunications service; other localities act through broadband or wireless authorities.

US-VT.note: Towns may form communications union districts that build and operate communications plant and deliver service; each town joins by voter approval.

US-WA.note: HB 1336 lifted the limits that kept public utility districts and other public entities from selling retail broadband; RCW 54.16.330 now authorizes retail telecommunications service.

US-WI.note: A city, village or town must hold a hearing and publish a three-year cost-benefit report before building a facility to serve the public, unless it shows the area lacks private broadband.

US-MA.note: No statewide ban. US-ME.note: P.L. 2025, c. 456 bars municipalities, unless another statute authorizes it, from prohibiting the heating or energy system a person chooses. It was a 2025 non-emergency law, presumably in force before 1/1/2026, but the effective date was not confirmed.

US-NC.note: S.L. 2023-58 (HB 130) became law without the governor's signature on 6/26/2023 and took effect then (https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/SessionLaws/HTML/2023-2024/SL2023-58.html).

US-ND.note: Cities and counties may not prohibit or impede a utility connection based on fuel source; enacted in 2023 (per the earlier draft), effective date not confirmed. County text at https://ndlegis.gov/cencode/t11c10.pdf.

US-AK.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-AL.note: People convicted of felonies involving moral turpitude must apply for restoration after completing the sentence and paying fines, fees and restitution; certain crimes (for example murder, rape, treason) are permanent bars unless pardoned.

US-AR.note: Fines, fees and restitution must be paid before the vote returns, so restoration is not automatic (the same rule as Florida).

US-AZ.note: First-time offenders are restored automatically on completion of probation or absolute discharge if victim restitution is paid; people with two or more felonies must obtain a pardon or court restoration.

US-CA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-CO.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-CT.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison. Election-law convictions bar voting until incarceration, probation and parole are complete.

US-DC.note: People never lose the right to vote for a criminal conviction; the former exclusion of people incarcerated for a felony (repealed in 2020) already restored the right on release.

US-DE.cite: Del. Const. art. V, § 2; 15 Del. C. § 6102
US-DE.note: Most people are restored automatically on completion of sentence, but disqualifying felonies (for example murder, bribery, sexual offenses) are a permanent bar unless pardoned, and election offenses carry a 10-year bar.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Stat. § 98.0751; Fla. Const. art. VI, § 4
US-FL.note: Amendment 4 as implemented by SB 7066 restores rights automatically only after completion of all terms of sentence, defined to include full payment of restitution and court-ordered fines and fees; murder and felony sexual offenses require clemency. The answer was also no before SB 7066 took effect on July 1, 2019.

US-GA.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-HI.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-IA.note: The constitution disenfranchises permanently; Governor Reynolds's executive order of August 5, 2020 automatically restores most people on completion of sentence, but certain homicide offenses need individual gubernatorial restoration, and the order is executive, not statutory.

US-ID.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-IL.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-IN.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-KS.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-KY.note: The constitution disenfranchises permanently; Governor Beshear's executive order of December 12, 2019 automatically restores most people who complete their sentence, but treason, election bribery and certain violent offenses require individual restoration.

US-LA.note: Rights return automatically no later than completion of sentence, and earlier for people on probation or parole who have not been incarcerated within the last five years; a person must show eligibility documentation when registering.

US-MA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MD.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison. A conviction for buying or selling votes is a permanent bar unless pardoned, a narrow election-crime exception.

US-ME.note: People never lose the right to vote for a criminal conviction, even while incarcerated.

US-MI.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MN.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MO.note: On 2026-01-01 rights returned automatically on completion of sentence; HB 1871 (effective August 28, 2026) restores most on release from prison; a felony or misdemeanor connected with the right of suffrage remains a permanent bar, treated here as a narrow election-crime exception.

US-MS.note: Specified disqualifying offenses are a permanent bar unless the governor pardons or both houses of the legislature restore the right by a two-thirds vote.

US-MT.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NC.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-ND.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NE.note: Disqualification is automatically removed on completion of the sentence including parole; Laws 2024, LB 20 repealed the former two-year waiting period (effective July 19, 2024, per the task brief; the exact date was not on a fetched page).

US-NH.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NJ.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NM.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NV.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NY.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-OH.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison. A person twice convicted of violating Ohio election law is permanently barred unless pardoned, a narrow election-crime exception.

US-OK.note: Automatic restoration upon completion, discharge or commutation of the original sentence, or a pardon.

US-OR.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-PA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison. A person convicted of violating Pennsylvania election law is barred for four years after conviction, a narrow election-crime exception.

US-RI.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-SC.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-SD.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-TN.note: People must obtain a court order after completing the sentence and paying restitution and meeting child-support obligations; certain felonies (for example rape, murder, bribery, treason) are permanent bars.

US-TX.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-UT.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-VA.note: On 2026-01-01 the constitution required restoration by the governor case by case; under Department of Elections guidance of September 15, 2026 most people are restored automatically on release from prison, while murder and manslaughter still require an application.

US-VT.note: People never lose the right to vote for a criminal conviction, even while incarcerated.

US-WA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-WI.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-WV.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-WY.note: Automatic restoration applies only to first-time nonviolent felonies in a Wyoming court completed on or after January 1, 2010; others must apply, and violent or multiple felonies are a permanent bar unless pardoned.

US-AK.note: No gestational limit; the Alaska Supreme Court recognizes a state constitutional right to abortion.

US-AL.note: Banned at all stages, with exceptions for serious risk to the patient's health and lethal fetal anomaly.

US-AR.note: Banned at all stages, with an exception only to save the patient's life.

US-AZ.note: After viability, except to preserve the patient's life or health; after 2024 Prop 139, the 15-week ban was permanently enjoined in March 2025.

US-CA.note: After viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-CO.note: No gestational limit; the Reproductive Health Equity Act and 2024 Amendment 79 protect abortion.

US-CT.note: After viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-DC.note: No gestational limit in District law.

US-DE.note: After viability, except for the patient's life or health or a fatal fetal anomaly.

US-FL.note: After about six weeks (fetal cardiac activity), with listed exceptions; the 2024 Amendment 4 ballot measure fell short of the 60% threshold.

US-GA.note: After about six weeks (fetal cardiac activity), with listed exceptions; a September 2024 trial ruling striking it was stayed by the Georgia Supreme Court, and the limit stayed in force.

US-HI.note: After viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-IA.note: After about six weeks (fetal cardiac activity), with listed exceptions; in force since July 29, 2024.

US-ID.note: Banned at all stages, with listed exceptions (life of the patient; reported rape or incest in the first trimester).

US-IL.note: After viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-IN.note: Banned at all stages, with narrow listed exceptions (life and serious health risk, lethal anomaly, rape or incest early in pregnancy).

US-KS.note: After 22 weeks (pain-capable limit), with listed exceptions.

US-KY.note: Banned at all stages, with an exception for life or serious health risk to the patient.

US-LA.note: Banned at all stages, with exceptions for life, serious health risk and listed medically futile pregnancies.

US-MA.note: After 24 weeks, with exceptions for life, health and fatal or grave fetal anomaly.

US-MD.note: No gestational limit in force; 2024 Question 1 added a constitutional right to reproductive freedom.

US-ME.note: After viability, unless a physician finds it medically necessary.

US-MI.note: No gestational limit; 2022 Proposal 3 allows post-viability regulation, but no such ban is in force.

US-MN.note: No gestational limit; the 2023 Protect Reproductive Options Act guarantees the right.

US-MO.note: After viability, except in a medical emergency or to preserve the patient's life or health; 2024 Amendment 3 ended the total ban, which a Jackson County court blocked again in July 2025 after the state Supreme Court vacated an earlier injunction. A repeal amendment is on the November 2026 ballot.

US-MP.cite: N. Mar. I. Const. art. I, § 12
US-MP.note: Banned at all stages by the constitution, except as provided by law.

US-MS.note: Banned at all stages, with exceptions for the patient's life and reported rape.

US-MT.note: After viability, except to preserve the patient's life or health; the 20-week limit was blocked and 2024 Initiative 128 added an abortion right.

US-NC.note: After 12 weeks, with longer windows for rape or incest (20 weeks) and life-limiting anomalies (24 weeks).

US-ND.note: Banned at all stages, with listed exceptions; a district court struck the ban in September 2024, but the North Dakota Supreme Court reinstated it in November 2025, so it was enforceable on 1/1/2026.

US-NE.note: After 12 weeks, with listed exceptions; 2024 Initiative 434 wrote the 12-week limit into the constitution.

US-NH.note: After 24 weeks, with exceptions for medical emergency and fatal fetal anomaly.

US-NJ.note: No gestational limit; the 2022 Freedom of Reproductive Choice Act.

US-NM.note: No gestational limit; the old criminal ban was repealed in 2021.

US-NV.note: After 24 weeks, except to preserve the patient's life or health; the 2024 constitutional amendment needs a second vote in November 2026.

US-NY.note: After 24 weeks or viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-OH.note: After 20 weeks post-fertilization (about 22 weeks), with exceptions; the six-week ban is blocked after 2023 Issue 1, which allows post-viability limits.

US-OK.note: Banned at all stages, with an exception to save the patient's life in a medical emergency.

US-PA.note: After 24 weeks, except to prevent the patient's death or serious health risk.

US-RI.note: After viability, except to preserve the patient's life or health.

US-SC.note: After about six weeks (fetal cardiac activity), with listed exceptions.

US-SD.note: Banned at all stages, with an exception to preserve the patient's life (amended in 2026 without changing the answer).

US-TN.note: Banned at all stages, with listed medical exceptions (life, serious health risk, ectopic and molar pregnancies).

US-TX.note: Banned at all stages, with an exception for a life-threatening physical condition or serious risk of major bodily impairment.

US-UT.note: After 18 weeks, with listed exceptions; the near-total trigger ban remains enjoined by state courts.

US-VA.note: In the third trimester, unless three physicians certify it is needed for the patient's life or health; a constitutional amendment is on the November 2026 ballot.

US-VT.note: No gestational limit; 2022 Article 22 added a constitutional right to reproductive autonomy.

US-WA.note: After viability, except to protect the patient's life or health.

US-WI.note: After 20 weeks post-fertilization (about 22 weeks), with a medical-emergency exception; the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in July 2025 that the 1849 law does not ban abortion.

US-WV.note: Banned at all stages, with exceptions for nonviable pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, medical emergency and reported rape or incest early in pregnancy.

US-WY.note: After viability, with a life or health exception; the 2023 total and pill bans were struck by a district court in November 2024 (affirmed January 6, 2026), and a six-week ban signed in March 2026 is after this date.

US-AK.note: Home-rule boroughs and cities may exercise all legislative powers not prohibited by law or charter, and the list of home-rule limits in AS 29.10.200 (checked at https://www.akleg.gov/basis/statutes.asp?media=print&secStart=29.10.200&secEnd=29.10.200) says nothing about wages; no Alaska city has yet adopted one.

US-AL.note: Signed February 25, 2016, voiding Birmingham's $10.10 ordinance; the Eleventh Circuit (en banc, 2019) dismissed the challenge for lack of standing.

US-AR.note: Act 643 of 2017 (approved 03/24/2017, no emergency clause) bars counties, cities and towns from requiring a minimum or living wage above state or federal law.

US-AZ.note: Counties, cities and towns may set higher minimum wages by ordinance; Flagstaff and Tucson have done so.

US-CA.note: No state preemption; about 40 cities and counties, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and San Diego, have their own higher minimum wages.

US-CO.note: H.B. 19-1210 repealed the prior ban on local minimum wages; Denver, Edgewater and Boulder County have since adopted them.

US-DC.note: D.C. has no state above it; the D.C. Council sets a local minimum wage above the federal rate (ordinance dates from 1992).

US-FL.note: The statute (ch. 2003-87) bars local minimum wages, though Fla. Const. art. X, § 24(f) says the amendment does not limit any public body from requiring higher wages; ch. 2024-80 tightens the ban (adds 'maintain' and contractor wage rules) effective 09/30/2026.

US-IA.note: Ordinances adopted before 03/30/2017 were voided, including the Johnson, Linn, Polk, Lee and Wapello County wages.

US-ID.note: Section history lists amendments in 2007 and 2016 (ch. 145); the exact date subsection (4) took effect was not confirmed.

US-IL.note: Home-rule units may set higher wages; Chicago and Cook County have (many Cook County municipalities have opted out of the county rate).

US-KS.note: Bars cities and counties from requiring wages above the minimum wage unless state or federal law requires them; enacted 2013 per NELP.

US-KY.cite: KRS 337.275 (as construed in Ky. Restaurant Ass'n v. Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Gov't, Ky. 2016)
US-KY.note: No express statute; the Kentucky Supreme Court held in 2016 that the state wage law leaves no room for local minimums, voiding the Louisville and Lexington ordinances.

US-MD.note: Montgomery and Howard Counties have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-ME.note: No state preemption found; Portland and Rockland have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-MI.note: Local Government Labor Regulatory Limitation Act, 2015 PA 105, immediate effect.

US-MN.note: Minneapolis and St. Paul have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-MO.note: H.B. 1194 & 1193 (2017) nullified the St. Louis ordinance after the state supreme court struck the older 1998 ban (RSMo 67.1571) on single-subject grounds.

US-MS.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state code text itself was not reachable.

US-MT.note: Self-government units are denied any power to require a private employer to pay a wage or benefit not required by state or federal law (subsection (2) also bars acting on Title 39, the labor title); the section history lists several 2021 amendments, and which one added (23) was not confirmed.

US-NC.note: Current subsection (d), added by S.L. 2023-134, s. 5.9(a), preempts local rules on private-employer pay; the earlier subsection (c) from the 2016 law was repealed by S.L. 2017-4.

US-ND.note: Weak: North Dakota applies Dillon's Rule (Wikipedia table) and home-rule cities get only the powers enumerated in § 40-05.1-06, which list no wage power; the general-welfare ordinance power in subsection 10 has not been tested on wages.

US-NH.note: Weak: New Hampshire follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table), and the town bylaw powers in RSA 31:39 (https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/III/31/31-39.htm) list no wage power.

US-NM.note: Santa Fe city and county, Las Cruces and Albuquerque have local minimum wages.

US-NV.note: Weak: Nevada keeps Dillon's Rule except for city 'matters of local concern', a term that excludes matters needing statewide uniformity and business activities subject to substantial state regulation, and no statute grants wage-setting power.

US-NY.cite: N.Y. Labor Law § 652 (as construed in Wholesale Laundry Bd. of Trade v. City of New York, 1962)
US-NY.note: No express statute; a 1962 court ruling holds cities cannot set their own minimum wage, and advocates argue it could be reconsidered; the higher NYC/Long Island/Westchester rates are set by state law.

US-OK.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the statute text was not reachable (oscn.net bot challenge).

US-OR.note: Enacted 2001 (ch. 967); local governments may set wages only for their own employees, contracts and subsidies; the Portland-metro, standard and nonurban tiers are set by state law (ORS 653.025).

US-PA.note: Philadelphia states it is preempted by Act 112 from passing any minimum wage law.

US-RI.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state statute site was not reachable from this environment.

US-SC.note: Enacted by 2002 Act No. 243; bars local minimum wages above the federal rate.

US-SD.note: Only home-rule charter units qualify: their ordinances may set standards higher than state law unless a state law provides otherwise, though SDCL 6-12-6(1) withholds power over private civil relationships and no local wage has been tested.

US-TN.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state code text was not reachable.

US-TX.note: The state minimum wage supersedes local wage ordinances for private employment, except public contracts.

US-UT.note: Cities, towns and counties may not require a minimum wage above the federal minimum; last amended 2005.

US-VA.cite: Va. Code § 15.2-1102 (charter powers, read under Dillon's Rule)
US-VA.note: Weak: Virginia follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table); the general-welfare charter powers in Va. Code § 15.2-1102 (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title15.2/chapter11/section15.2-1102/) grant no wage power in terms, and no Virginia locality has one.

US-VT.note: Weak: Vermont follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table), and the enumerated municipal powers in 24 V.S.A. § 2291 include no power to set wages.

US-WA.note: State law is a floor that leaves more favorable local wage ordinances in force; Seattle, SeaTac, Tukwila and others have higher rates.

US-WI.note: 2005 Wis. Act 12 voided any local minimum wage ordinance in effect on June 16, 2005 (Madison's).
